title: "I Feel Like A Loser Right After Winning"
subtitle: Thinking carefully about narcissism after a slow news day.
body_html:
The Frontier Psychiatrists is a daily health-themed newsletter. Yesterday was a very slow news day. I had to come up with some completely out of the blue content. Today, I'm going to address narcissism. Not the narcissism of disrepute on the Internet. This is not an article about "the narcissist" or “narcissistic abuse.” It's not about other people. It's about me. It's about you. It's about us. All of us have a personality. That personality includes a variety of different dimensions, and I like to break up personality functioning in my mind into four domains. I didn't make this up; it comes from the DSM-5’s alternate dimensional model of personality disorders.

This model conceptualizes personality function across the domains of:

  • Identity

  • Self-Direction

  • Empathy

  • Intimacy

It lays out, quite nicely, what impairment looks like across those dimensions. Personality traits are not necessarily good or bad in and of themselves. Let's take a look at healthy narcissism and where it can cross over the line to unhealthy or pathological.

In individuals with higher degrees of healthy narcissism, a positive sense of self is paired with a sense of grandiosity. These individuals can have higher degrees of self-centeredness but also believe themselves capable of remarkable things. There is often an “antagonistic core” of that individual’s personality.

If we were breaking one of these individuals down on dimensions, they might have a strong sense of who they are and what they're doing, but they may show impairments in domains related to empathy and intimacy. In some context, let's say you're the CEO of a startup, and the organization's finances require you to lay off staff. Many people would feel very bad about this. Some might even kick the can down the road or not fire people even when they can't afford to keep them on staff. This can lead to the destruction of that company, no matter how promising because they kept people on longer than was financially viable. In this context, empathy, feeling the emotions and pain of others, and intimacy, feeling deeply connected to others, can get in the way of what you need to do. And that's fire people, some of the time.

Individuals with a higher degree of grandiose narcissism might care less about the individual employees and more about their brilliant vision for the future. Thus, they might be able to act more rapidly and decisively to preserve the resources of the company that they know, in their hearts, will change the world for the better, like every revolutionary disruptive platform solution—is there any other kind?

By chance, some of the time, these narcissistic founders will be correct. Their company will turn out to be important. The firings were a good idea. It was their brilliance— or just a twist of fate; they'll turn out to be correct in retrospect. These personality traits are adaptive, sometimes.

To be frank, sometimes, it's helpful not to give a “flying F” about other people. Not everybody should be so callous. Not everybody will be in roles where this might be adaptive. The thing I've said about it for a while? “Without grandiosity—the sense that you can do things that other people think are impossible—the only job would be accounting. Shooting for the stars isn’t prudent.

If it wasn't for mania, narcissism, and ADHD, nothing cool would happen, ever.

Now, there are times when that goes poorly. There is a trade-off that comes with narcissistic personality traits. Although individuals can feel driven to accomplish the impossible, their goals are often impossible. And even when their goals are possible, you still might not feel good no matter how remarkable the accomplishment.

Grandiose individuals, and I will admit to being one, strive. I'm a major striver. I'm big on striving. Have I told you about how much I strive? The problem? It is built into this ambitious goal-setting. As I reviewed in my article on objectives and key results, for some of us, accomplishing a goal means we didn't set ambitious enough goals. Meeting your goals is failure in the minds of some. Never good enough!

This is a horrible trap! It's also pretty heritable (a.k.a. genetic). If you look at narcissistic personality disorder, the version of a narcissistic personality trait that crosses the line from adaptive to pathological, we see the heritability is on the order of 0.711. Narcissistic personality disorder is more heritable than depression, more heritable than borderline personality disorder, more than bipolar disorder.2

If you imagine the above personality dimensions each with more impairment? It looks like the following—when it comes to identity, imagine being unsure of who you are in the context of a failure. In the domain of self-direction, it can look like you're unclear about why you're doing anything if it isn't about becoming famous or rich or renowned.

Glenn Gabbard tells the story—in his book Narcissism and Its Discontents (affiliate link)— of a patient who is a Nobel Prize winner who came into the office for therapy after getting one of the most prestigious awards in the world and told his therapist he felt like a loser nothing unless he won another Nobel. Only two people have ever won two Nobel prizes.

Narcissism has an extremely broad range of impairments. Unfortunately, at its extremes, or in the wrong context.—that of confronting failure, for example—it can become fatal. Rates of suicide attempts and completions and individuals with NPD are higher.3 Among personality pathology, only narcissistic personality disorder is a driver of multiple suicide attempts.

Narcissism is Both a personality trait that can be part of a healthy person, and it can lead to severe and deviating impairments for both the individual and—crucially—others in the world. At the extreme range of pathology, mixed with antisocial features and psychopathy—narcissistic personality disorder is a horrific and destructive force. Anyone who has seen stalkers depicted in the popular press knows some individuals feel entitled to do whatever they want for them, other social norms be damned.

This is not a call to shun this personality trait, it’s a call to think about personality and how to deliver effective treatments, some of which require more development, to address the suffering of individuals impacted. Which, I think one could note, could be all of us, if such individuals end up in positions of power or influence over our lives.

1

Torgersen, S., Myers, J., Reichborn-Kjennerud, T., Røysamb, E., Kubarych, T. S., & Kendler, K. S. (2012). The heritability of Cluster B personality disorders assessed both by personal interview and questionnaire. Journal of Personality Disorders, 26(6), 848-866.

2

Luo, Y. L., & Cai, H. (2018). The etiology of narcissism: A review of behavioral genetic studies. Handbook of Trait Narcissism: Key Advances, Research Methods, and Controversies, 149-156.

3

Ansell, E. B., Wright, A. G., Markowitz, J. C., Sanislow, C. A., Hopwood, C. J., Zanarini, M. C., ... & Grilo, C. M. (2015). Personality disorder risk factors for suicide attempts over 10 years of follow-up. Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment, 6(2), 161.
